readingInstruction: Read 2 Corinthians 6:1-9:15. These four chapters hold several themes: the day of salvation, holiness and separation, godly grief and repentance, and generous giving. Read the appeal for the collection in chapters 8 and 9 slowly, noticing its motive.
settingTheScene: Paul continues his defense of the ministry and moves to appeals. He urges the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain, to pursue holiness, and to complete their promised gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Titus has brought news that the church repented after Paul’s painful letter, and Paul rejoices. The collection in chapters 8 and 9 is the longest discussion of Christian giving in the New Testament.
observation: “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (6:2).
“As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything” (6:10).
“For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (7:10).
“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (8:9).
“For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (8:12).
“Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (9:6).
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (9:7).
“Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (9:15).
interpretation:
Paul urges the Corinthians, as God’s fellow workers, not to receive the grace of God in vain. Quoting Isaiah 49:8, he says, “Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” He then describes his own ministry through a list of hardships and virtues: afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger; by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love, truthful speech, and the power of God. “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” The Christian life is full of paradox.

Then comes a call to holiness: “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” This is not a call to withdraw from the world but to avoid being joined to what contradicts our devotion to Christ. The reason: “For we are the temple of the living God.” God promises, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them… I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me.” The chapter ends with the call to cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

In chapter 7, Paul rejoices that the church responded to his painful letter. “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.” Worldly grief is sorrow at being caught; godly grief is sorrow at sinning against God. Titus was refreshed by their response, and Paul’s joy is complete.

Chapters 8 and 9 speak of the collection. The Macedonian churches, in a severe test of affliction, with abundance of joy and extreme poverty, overflowed in a wealth of generosity. They gave beyond their means, begging earnestly for the favor of taking part. Notice the order: “They gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.” Giving flows from devotion. Then the ground of all giving: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.” The incarnation is the model of generosity. Paul does not command but tests the sincerity of their love. Principles: give willingly, according to what you have, so that there may be fairness. Transparency and accountability are important: Titus and others will handle the funds so that no one can criticize.

Chapter 9 gives encouragement. “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.” “Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” This does not promise material wealth in return; the harvest is righteousness and thanksgiving. “God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.” Quoting Psalm 112:9, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” The result of generosity is thanksgiving to God. The chapter ends with praise: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” The ultimate gift is Christ.
connection: Isaiah 49:8 is quoted in 6:2. Leviticus 26:11-12 and Ezekiel 37:27 stand behind 6:16. Psalm 112:9 is quoted in 9:9. Acts 11:27-30 and Romans 15:25-27 describe the collection. Philippians 2:5-8 shows Christ’s self-emptying. Philippians 4:10-20 speaks of the Philippians’ gift. Luke 21:1-4 records the widow’s offering. Proverbs 11:24-25 and 22:9 speak of generosity. Matthew 6:19-21 says where your treasure is, there your heart will be. Psalm 51:17 and Luke 18:13 show true repentance.
application:
Choose an amount to give that stretches you. Do it cheerfully, not by compulsion.

Distinguish worldly grief from godly grief in your own heart. Are you sorry for the sin, or for the consequences?

Meditate on 8:9 and remember the cost of Christ’s generosity to you.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for becoming poor so that you might become rich.
Ask him to make you cheerful in giving.
Tell him how you want to give this week.
